description: Sparassis crispa, the cauliflower mushroom, is a distinctive wood-rotting fungus that forms a large, rounded, cream to pale-yellow rosette composed of many flattened, wavy, ribbon-like lobes, superficially resembling a head of cauliflower or a bath sponge. Fruitbodies arise at the base of conifers (chiefly pines) or from nearby roots, where the fungus causes a brown root and butt rot. The flesh is firm and tough when young, with a pleasant aromatic smell. Specimens can be substantial, commonly 10-40 cm across and weighing up to several kilograms. It is a prized choice edible, but the intricate folds readily trap soil, needles, and insects, so it must be cleaned thoroughly and cooked well before eating.
edibilityNotes: A choice edible when young, firm, and cream-colored. Discard older specimens that have yellowed and toughened. The convoluted lobes trap pine debris and insects, so clean meticulously and cook thoroughly; it is not eaten raw. As with any wild mushroom, eat only a small amount the first time to check personal tolerance, and rely on a verified identification before consuming.
distribution: Widespread across temperate regions of Europe (e.g. Britain, Scandinavia, Germany, Poland), North America, and Asia, fruiting where suitable conifer (especially pine) hosts occur.

dangerousLookalikes.name: Sparassis spathulata
dangerousLookalikes.note: A closely related cauliflower mushroom with broader, flatter, more erect leaf-like lobes (rather than narrow wavy ribbons), typically at the base of hardwoods such as oak and beech (occasionally pines). Also edible, so confusion is not dangerous, but it is a separate species.
